UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                            )

     American Transmission Company LLC                      )            Docket No. ER26-3265

                                                            )


        COMMENTS OF THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF WISCONSIN

           Pursuant to Rule 214(a)(2) of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (Commission), the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin (PSCW)

filed and served on July 31, 2026 a notice of intervention in the Section 205 filing of American

Transmission Company LLC (ATC) in this docket. The PSCW now respectfully submits these

comments on ATC’s filing.

           These comments focus on the Large Load Project Commitment Agreements (LLPCAs)

between ATC and Wisconsin Electric Power Company (WEPCO) proposed by ATC’s filing and

on ATC’s existing cost allocation framework. These comments do not opine on ATC’s proposed

Minimum Transmission Charge Agreement (MTCA). These comments are based solely on the

information in Docket No. ER26-3265 and are to be considered entirely separate from pending

affiliated interest agreement applications before the PSCW. 1

      I.          ATC’s Existing Zonal Cost Allocation Method Shifts Large Load
                  Interconnection Costs to Other Wholesale Customers.
           ATC’s filing attempts to address only two of the problems that exist with respect to the

shifting of network upgrade costs associated with large load interconnection (“large load costs”).

First, ATC’s filing addresses an issue unique to ATC wherein other wholesale transmission


1
  These comments do not address the merits of the ATC and WEPCO affiliated interest agreement applications
relating to the LLPCAs and MTCA, which were filed in PSCW Docket Nos. 5-AE-246 and 5-AE-284.

                                                       1
 customers pay financing costs while network upgrades are constructed through construction

work in progress (CWIP) accounting treatment. Second, ATC’s filing addresses an issue that

exists throughout the industry: attempting to prevent the risk of cost shifts when large loads do

not materialize as anticipated.

        There is, however, a very real potential for large load costs to be shifted onto other ATC

wholesale transmission customers even if the CWIP issue is addressed and load materializes

exactly as anticipated. While the PSCW considers ATC’s filing an improvement upon their

existing tariff as it relates to cost allocation issues, as explained and qualified further below, these

comments should not be interpreted as support for ATC’s existing tariff and its zonal cost

allocation for large loads. “Speed to Power” must not be used as an excuse to turn a blind eye to

cost causation principles that provide critical consumer protection. The scale of upgrades, size of

incremental costs, and other unique features associated with large load network upgrades—

including but not limited to providing service to a single customer, operational reliability

considerations, and potential for additional future upgrades—must all be considered when

determining an appropriate cost allocation.

        The Commission properly identified these cost-shifting risks in its Midcontinent

Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) Show Cause Order in Docket No. EL26-70 (“206

proceeding”), requiring additional information be made available for state regulators and

requesting additional insights into the nature of the transmission cost allocation issue. 2 The

PSCW does not believe that additional information alone will be sufficient to overcome the

structural hurdles in the Commission-approved MISO tariff; nor can the PSCW reallocate FERC-



2
 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”), ¶¶ 70 and
125.

                                                     2
 jurisdictional costs in the retail ratemaking process. Large load customers simply cannot be made

responsible for the costs they cause to the system without stronger Commission action on this

front.

           The 206 proceeding creates the expectation that individual transmission owners will be

voluntarily making 205 filings related to local project cost allocation. Solutions to these cost shift

issues were contemplated in the original record of the large load Advanced Notice of Proposed

Rulemaking (ANOPR) in Docket No. RM26-4 but were not directly addressed by the

Commission. The PSCW appreciates the recognition that state-federal collaboration is required

to achieve this result and provides these comments in support of speedy development of a

reasonable outcome.

           In recent PSCW Docket No. 6630-TE-113, the retail ratemaking proceeding on

WEPCO’s application for approval of its Very Large Customer (VLC) and bespoke resources

tariffs, the PSCW analyzed large load costs and their project-dependent nature for the large load

that is the subject of the instant filing. A copy of the PSCW’s Final Decision in that proceeding

is included as Attachment A. Relevant testimony by PSCW staff and WEPCO is included as

Attachments B, C, and D.

           In that retail tariff proceeding, analysis provided by WEPCO and PSCW staff compared

VLC-related transmission cost allocation under traditional zonal rates (termed “Load Ratio

Share”) to VLC-related transmission cost allocation under direct assignment. 3 The Load Ratio

Share methodology is allowed under the Commission-approved ATC Tariff. The Load Ratio

Share methodology was compared with how costs would be allocated if the VLC was directly

network upgrades to existing embedded rates. Two different customers were analyzed: a

hypothetical customer as defined by the applicant and an actual prospective VLC informed by

executed Payment and Cancellation Agreements (PCAs). The two main differences between the

customers were required network upgrade costs and their maximum requested interconnection

capacity. Both methods assume full-load materialization that is representative of the filed

agreement. The hypothetical customer was found to pay more than its directly assignable costs

through zonal rates at the 10-year mark as shown in Table 1.

            To be clear, the PSCW does not share this analysis as a means to advocate for direct

assignment of large load costs in lieu of large loads paying zonal rates. The analysis highlights

how a cost-causer evaluation of large load costs reveals the project-dependent nature and the

scale of harm that can result from failing to properly analyze and assign these costs. This analysis

shows that reliance on zonal rates, even when based on maximum requested interconnection

capacity, does not ensure large load customers are ultimately held responsible for the true costs

they cause by failing to prevent cost shifting to other wholesale transmission customers.

           As noted in ATC’s filing, “[t]he MTCA does not amend, change, or otherwise impact

ATC’s recovery of T-D Project costs from WEPCO through monthly payments associated with

Schedule 9-ATC.” Stated another way, the collection of bilateral agreements between ATC and

WEPCO in the instant filing leaves MISO’s existing Schedule 9 and its associated zonal cost

allocation intact, which prevents state regulators from ensuring other customers do not pay for

large load costs. If ATC’s filing is approved, the Commission should make it abundantly clear

that the issues associated with shifting large load costs to other wholesale customers through

zonal cost allocation, even when load materializes as planned, remains an open issue in the 206

proceeding.

           For these reasons and due to the limited time to review ATC’s filing, the PSCW takes no

position on whether the instant filing is “fair to and protective of ATC’s other wholesale

customers.” 4 As discussed further below, the PSCW takes the position that the agreements

contained within ATC’s filing are more fair and more protective than what is afforded by the

existing tariff.




4
    ATC filing at 7.

                                                   5
      II.          The Commission Should Accept the Filing and Continue a Comprehensive
                  Section 206 Investigation.
           The PSCW is supportive of Commission acceptance of the instant filing because it is

readily apparent that the key elements of the filing are directionally appropriate and present an

improvement on ATC’s existing tariff. The filing takes the first steps toward remedying serious

flaws in existing large load cost allocation – some of which are unique to ATC – and it reduces

risks borne by other wholesale transmission customers. For these reasons, the PSCW is

supportive of Commission acceptance of the filing and urges the Commission to authorize the

requested July 1, 2026 effective date. The retroactive effective date is appropriate due to the

bilateral nature of the agreements filed and is necessary to better allocate to the cost causers the

costs already incurred.

           It is critically important that the Commission clarify that acceptance of these agreements

does none of the following:

                  a. Absolve ATC of other actions that may be required pursuant to the ongoing
                     206 investigation in Docket No. EL26-70;
                  b. Prejudge whether further reforms are required under the Show Cause Order;
                     nor
                  c. Prevent the Commission from establishing a different replacement tariff after
                     further development of the record in the 206 proceeding.
           While these agreements would provide immediate, limited protection, the Commission

must consider whether it is reasonable to allow a series of one-off voluntary agreements to

address such a large portion of a transmission owner’s total revenue requirement. The PSCW

believes that the ongoing 206 proceeding is the appropriate venue in which to grapple with this

very question. It is critically important that the Commission make clear that all issues raised in

the Show Cause Order remain active and require additional evidence and support.

           PSCW Support for Monthly CWIP Charge and Further Investigation


                                                    6
         Perhaps the most important component of ATC’s filing is the proposed fix, housed within

the Revised LLPCAs, that attempts to remedy the unreasonable CWIP treatment afforded to all

of ATC’s transmission projects. 5 The existing formula rate treatment approved by the

Commission allows all ATC wholesale transmission customers to pay to finance the buildout of

new infrastructure that is required to serve large loads. Granting the treatment for all ATC

projects to earn a current return on CWIP is unique amongst transmission owners within MISO.

To be clear, ATC’s CWIP treatment for network upgrades is an example of the structures

currently in place that prompted the Commission’s preliminary finding that the transmission rates

are no longer just and reasonable because they shift risks and do not ensure customers are

ultimately responsible for the costs they cause.

        Billion-dollar investments and gigawatt-scale loads have the potential to shift tens to

hundreds of millions of dollars in financing costs to the wrong customers. Each of the LLPCAs

in ATC’s filing includes an Exhibit C that contains estimates of CWIP charges, beginning on July

1, 2026. Absent approval of the agreements proposed here and authorization of an effective date

of July 1, 2026, over $39 million in financing costs would be incorrectly spread to all of ATC’s

existing transmission customers. Notably, this cost does not include sizeable investments that

have already been made and are already in service for this customer, which means a portion of

these costs were already inappropriately spread to other transmission customers.

        Whether or not the Commission finds it reasonable to leave the CWIP framework in

place for large load network upgrades, in the 206 proceeding ATC should be required to justify

allowing for massive shifts of financing costs until the establishment of voluntary agreements



5
  To be clear, the PSCW believes the CWIP treatment is unreasonable only for network upgrades identified to serve
large loads. The PSCW does not oppose this treatment for other transmission projects.

                                                        7
 with its wholesale transmission customer. Again, the PSCW supports the agreements set forth in

this docket but does not view them as the durable, final solution.

       PSCW Support for Mechanisms that Protect Customers from Stranded Assets

       The PSCW generally supports mechanisms that reduce the risk of cost shifts caused by

load not materializing in accordance with planned timing or magnitude. ATC proposes the

Revised LLPCAs and the MTCA as two such protective mechanisms. Whether either one

adequately addresses the cost shift risk to other wholesale transmission customers requires

additional transparency around how project-specific network upgrades will be identified, as well

as consideration of how these mechanisms contribute to an overall just and reasonable rate for

transmission service. The PSCW appreciates that the Commission has enabled precisely this type

of consideration through the 206 proceeding.

       PSCW Support for Additional Transparency

       While it is clear that ATC’s filing was not intended to address all categories of reform

raised by the Commission in the 206 proceeding, examination of the relationship between those

unaddressed areas and the agreements contained within ATC’s filing is important. Without

addressing the transparency concerns raised by the Commission in the 206 proceeding, ATC’s

filing – on its own – does not ensure the resulting transmission rates are just and reasonable. For

example, the projects identified in the agreements in this docket, while necessary to serve a large

load customer, have been self-selected by WEPCO and ATC and do not match the list of projects

identified and approved by MISO as needed for a reliable interconnection of this very load. In

2024, ATC submitted to MISO two separate Expedited Project Review (EPR) requests for the

new large load customer contemplated in the instant filing that resulted in eight projects

identified as necessary to address reliability issues caused by the load’s interconnection.

                                                 8
 However, there are only four projects included in the LLPCAs, and these four do not correspond

with the results of the MISO study process. Further, the PSCW has permitted numerous projects

identified as needed to serve this large load that are not covered by the LLPCAs.

       Additionally, no load values (e.g., interconnection capacity requested, interconnection

capacity studied, and interconnection capacity ultimately provided) were made available when

the EPR results were shared at the MISO Planning Advisory Committee, and none are publicly

available now. The Minimum Transmission Charge (MTC) proposed in ATC’s filing is calculated

based on the maximum amount of transmission capacity enabled by specific network upgrades,

but ATC seeks privileged treatment of the transmission capacity schedule in this filing, meaning

information is not transparently available outside of ATC’s filing. Thus the information gap

identified by the Commission via the 206 proceeding is relevant and applicable here.

       ATC’s recently created Large Load Cost Allocation Business Practice appears to be a first

attempt at providing greater visibility into this process. The Business Practice, which governs

cost allocation of transmission facilities needed to serve a large load customer, does not require

public posting of the network upgrades needed to serve a new large customer’s requested

transmission capacity as identified through the required system impact study. The identified

network upgrades, and their costs, are used to develop the scope and terms of LLPCAs to

mitigate cost shifting during construction, create the MTC Liability Cap, and help set the security

obligation to mitigate cost shifting if a new large customer does not materialize. While not taking

a position on the MTCA, the PSCW maintains that the transparency requirements proposed in

the 206 proceeding would clearly have value here. Without a clear, comprehensive list of

necessary upgrades to serve a large load, the reasonableness of the MTCA cannot be properly

evaluated. This highlights the interrelated nature of the categories of reform the Commission has


                                                 9
 identified in the 206 proceeding and underscores why all issues must remain subject to

investigation going forward even if the instant filing is approved.

       III.          Clarification Regarding “PSCW Direction”
              Because ATC has characterized the filing here as “responsive to PSCW direction,” the

PSCW wishes to clarify that the “direction” provided by the PSCW to ATC was limited and

indirect. Through WEPCO’s large load tariff retail ratemaking proceeding, the PSCW gave

direction to WEPCO to keep the PSCW apprised of developments related to transmission cost

allocation and ordered additional reporting on the impact large load network upgrades have on

ATC’s revenue requirement.6 The PSCW noted that it had limited ability to protect other

customers from paying for the infrastructure required to serve new large loads, highlighting all of

the cost shifting concerns under the Commission’s jurisdiction. The PSCW therefore anticipates

that this cost shifting will be addressed in the 206 proceeding.

              While the Commission has suggested additional transparency into the Network Upgrades

required to interconnect new large loads within its 206 proceeding, the Commission should order

additional reporting like the requirement the PSCW placed on WEPCO. This reporting should

include a clear $/MW analysis that demonstrates how large load costs compare to the existing

zonal rate. This clear comparison on $/MW terms will show whether any particular large load

puts upward or downward pressure on transmission rates.

       IV.           Conclusion
              ATC’s filing is an improvement upon the status quo, as the Revised LLPCAs meet the

requirements of FPA Section 205 and begin to remedy serious flaws in existing large load cost

allocation. However, ATC’s filing is far from fully responsive to the Commission’s Show Cause


6

                                                            10
 Order in Docket No. EL26-70, and additional work is needed to achieve just and reasonable

transmission rates. Specifically, the agreements proposed herein leave MISO’s existing Schedule

9 zonal cost allocation intact. As a result, the shifting of large load costs to other wholesale

customers through zonal cost allocation, even when load materializes as planned, remains an

unresolved issue. Thus, the PSCW requests that, should the Commission accept ATC’s filing in

this docket, the Commission should also clarify that its acceptance does not relieve ATC of other

actions that may be required by the ongoing 206 investigation in Docket No. EL26-70, does not

prejudge whether further reforms are required under the Show Cause Order, and does not prevent

the Commission from establishing a different replacement tariff after further development of the

record in the Show Cause proceeding.

       The PSCW encourages the Commission to remain steadfast in its undertaking in the

Show Cause proceeding to ensure that RTOs and transmission owners do not merely minimally

improve on transmission rates and terms of service that are no longer reasonable in the face of

new large load interconnection. ATC’s filing, along with the PSCW’s comments, serves only as

one incremental step in the Commission’s continued collection of evidence in the Show Cause

proceeding. The PSCW appreciates the opportunity to provide its perspective here.

                                        FINAL DECISION


       This is the Final Decision in the proceeding conducted by the Public Service Commission

of Wisconsin (Commission) on the application of Wisconsin Electric Power Company

(applicant) for approval of its Very Large Customer (VLC) and Bespoke Resources tariffs. The

application consists of a proposed VLC Market Pricing tariff and accompanying Electric Service

Agreement template and a proposed Bespoke Resources tariff and accompanying Resource

Service Agreement template.

       The VLC and Bespoke Resources tariffs are APPROVED, subject to conditions and as

modified by this Final Decision.


                                           Introduction

       The VLC tariff is proposed as a tariff mandatory for very large energy users and also

requires that VLC customers subscribe to specific resources under the proposed Bespoke

Resources tariff. The Bespoke Resources tariff requires any customer taking service under the

VLC tariff to enter into long-term agreements to subscribe to energy and capacity resources to

reduce long-term reliability on purchasing power through wholesale markets. Bespoke

Resources may include facilities such as new generators, storage facilities, or other resources, in

order to meet the large demand being added to the system by VLCs. The applicant’s proposed

tariffs and service agreements are intended to meet the significant energy and capacity needs of

VLCs while ensuring the VLCs pay for the infrastructure investments needed to serve them and
 avoid cross subsidization by other customers. The VLC and Bespoke Resources tariffs and

service agreements include long-term contractual commitments and additional financial

protections not present in the applicant’s other tariffs.


                                      Procedural Background

Agreements. (PSC REF#: 539747.)

The notice advised that a hearing would be scheduled at a later date. The notice instructed those

On August 6, 2025, Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Michael E. Newmark issued an Order on

                                        Findings of Fact

       1.      The applicant is an investor-owned electric, natural gas, and steam public utility

as defined in Wis. Stat. §196.01(5)(a). The applicant provides electric, natural gas, and steam

service in eastern Wisconsin.

       2.      It is reasonable to require the applicant to modify the VLC tariff to include an

initial term length of 15 years.

       3.      It is reasonable to make the VLC tariff mandatory for all customers with an

aggregate load forecast of 100 MW or more.


                                                 4
           4.    It is reasonable to require VLCs to subscribe to a sufficient amount of Bespoke

Resources to avoid long-term reliance on Fleet Firm or Market Firm Service resources.

          5.    It is reasonable to include a Fleet Firm Service Charge to be based on the Cp1

Billed Demand charge, less allocated transmission costs in the VLC tariff.

          6.    It is reasonable to require the applicant to estimate excess capacity of

non-participating customers using the applicant’s proposed method in advance of the Planning

Resource Auction (PRA).

          7.    It is reasonable to require the applicant to report, in future rate cases, the method

used to allocate fleet firm resources between multiple VLCs, if multiple VLCs are taking service.

          8.    It is reasonable to include a mandatory Insufficient Capacity Charge in the VLC

tariff.

          9.    It is reasonable for the Insufficient Capacity Charge to trigger when a VLC has a

capacity shortage in any season for three consecutive years.

          10.   It is not reasonable to require an Insufficient Energy Charge in the VLC tariff.

          11.   It is reasonable for the Transmission Service Charge to recover transmission costs

associated with serving a VLC based on a load ratio share methodology in conjunction with a

minimum billing demand level of 100 percent of initially forecasted load, or actual demand

during the billing period, whichever is higher.

          12.   It is reasonable to require the applicant to defer to the applicant’s next rate

proceeding the difference for any month where the Transmission Service Charge that was billed

to the applicant through the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s (MISO) Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC)-approved Open Access Transmission, Energy and

          13.   It is reasonable to set the terms of transmission cost recovery through the VLC

          14.   It is not reasonable to require the applicant to modify the VLC tariff to collect

transmission costs upfront.

          15.   It is reasonable for the Administrative Charges of the VLC tariff to be subject to

          16.   It is reasonable to require the applicant to provide detail regarding the

          17.   It is reasonable to require the VLC tariff to include waiver language that requires

          18.   It is reasonable to require the VLC tariff to be modified to add waiver language

 Applicable Standard of Review

        The Commission’s authority to establish utility rates and terms of service has a robust

statutory foundation. Wisconsin Stat. §§ 196.03, 196.20, and 196.37 grant the Commission its

general authority to establish utility rates and terms of service. Section 196.03 provides that any

public utility rate “shall be reasonable and just and every unjust or unreasonable charge for such

service is prohibited and declared unlawful.” Under § 196.20, “no change in schedules which

constitutes an increase in rates to consumers may be made except by order of the [C]ommission,

after an investigation and opportunity for hearing.” Under § 196.37, if the Commission finds

rates to be “unjust, unreasonable, insufficient or unjustly discriminatory or preferential or

otherwise unreasonable or unlawful, the [C]ommission shall determine and order reasonable

rates . . . to be imposed, observed and followed in the future.” The Commission’s evaluation of

the reasonableness of rates necessarily implicates numerous competing considerations, including

reliability, conservation, financial health of the utility (capital structure and rate of return),

customer affordability, and more.

        Rate setting is an area in which the Commission has special expertise. Brookfield v.

Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage Dist.,141 Wis. 2d 10, 15, 414 N.W.2d 308 (Ct. App. 1987).

It has set utility rates for more than 100 years. In ratemaking, the Commission exercises a

legislative function. Wis. Mfr. And Commerce v. Public Serv. Comm 'n (WMC),94 Wis. 2d 314,

319, 319, 287 N.W.2d 844 (1979).

        It is well established that the [Commission], in designing a rate structure that will
        enable a utility to recover the total revenue authorized, has wide discretion in
        determining the factors upon which it may base its precise rate schedule. . .
        Rate-making agencies are not bound to any single regulatory formula; they are
        permitted to make the pragmatic adjustments, which may be called for by
        particular circumstances, unless their statutory authority plainly precludes this.



                                                   12
 Id. at 320, (citing City of West Allis v Pub. Serv. Comm 'n, 42 Wis. 2d 569, 167 N.W.2d 401

(1969) (footnotes omitted).

         Determining whether rates are just and reasonable often requires a high degree of

discretion, judgment, and technical analysis. Such decisions involve intertwined legal, factual,

and public policy determinations. The Commission, as fact finder, is charged with sifting

through all of the information to reach a well-reasoned decision. In doing so, the Commission

uses its experience, technical competence, and specialized knowledge to determine the

credibility of each witness and the persuasiveness of highly technical evidence presented on each

issue.

         Wisconsin Stat. § 196.192 allows investor-owned electric public utilities to offer

market-based rates and individual contract-based rates. Such market-based rates must: 1) “result

in customers receiving market-based compensation for voluntary interruptions of firm load

during peak periods of electric use;” and 2) “include market-based pricing options and options

for individual contracts that allow a retail customer . . . to receive market benefits and take

market risks for the customer’s purchases of capacity or energy.” Wis. Stat. § 196.192(2)(bm).

The Commission may not approve a market-based rate “unless the [C]omission determines that

the rate will not harm shareholders of the investor-owned electric public utility or customers who

are not subject to the rate.” Wis. Stat. § 196.192(2)(br). Absent such a finding, the Commission

is required to approve market-based rate proposals that are consistent with the statute.

         Wisconsin Stat. § 196.192 does not define “harm” to shareholders or customers who are

not subject to the rate. The Commission has previous experience evaluating market-based rates

and in those instances has found that a proposal does not harm customers not subject to the rate




                                                  13
 “if they do not pay higher rates as a result.”1 Similarly, the Commission has viewed that

“shareholders will not be harmed if the [rate] does not diminish the [utility’s] net income or

expose the utility to greater risk.”2 The analysis of the proposal in this docket is further

complicated by the new and novel nature of both the type and scale of customers as well as the

applicant’s proposed framework for serving such customers. The Commission is being asked to

establish a rate prior to VLC customers taking full service and without the benefit of historical

operational data on the actual costs and revenues associated with serving such customers. The

Commission generally uses the framework established in past dockets applying Wis. Stat.

§ 196.192 as a guide for examining the applicant’s proposal for any risks presented to both

non-participating customers and shareholders.

VLC Tariff Term Length

ten-year period the term would be automatically renewed in one-year terms. For a customer to
